briefing.text: Check the coding of PRIOR_CHEMOTHERAPY in data_clinical_supplement.txt before using it. The library reports that its # description line defines 1 = chemotherapy NOT received and 0 = received, which is the reverse of the usual convention. Read the description line yourself and cross-tabulate PRIOR_CHEMOTHERAPY against PRIOR_CHEMO_CYCLES: cycles should be 0 exactly in the no-chemo group. Then recode to an explicit variable (e.g. chemo_received) before any comparison, and report any rows where the two columns disagree and how you handled them.
briefing.reason: If the exposure is read the wrong way round, the direction of the comparison flips, and so does the label.

briefing.text: The sample table may hold several samples per patient (e.g. primary and metastasis). Count samples per PATIENT_ID, check that merges between the sample, patient and supplement tables are one-to-one or many-to-one, and look for patients missing from any table. If patients have several samples, do not treat each sample as independent. Use one sample per patient (e.g. the primary, or the patient mean) or a mixed model with a patient random effect, and report the result both ways.
briefing.reason: Pseudoreplication makes p-values too small and gives extra weight to patients with many samples, which can create apparent significance.

briefing.text: Sample type (primary vs metastasis) can confound the chemotherapy comparison: immune infiltration differs by sample type, and pretreated patients may contribute more metastatic samples. Cross-tabulate chemo status by SAMPLE_TYPE and compare immune scores by SAMPLE_TYPE. If they are associated, stratify or adjust for it, and check that the chemo effect keeps the same direction within each stratum (Simpson's paradox).
briefing.reason: Unbalanced sample type can produce, hide or reverse a group difference.

briefing.text: Expression-based immune scores track tumour purity: samples with lower purity tend to score higher on immune infiltration. Correlate IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE with TUMOR_PURITY and compare purity between chemo groups. If there is an imbalance, report both the unadjusted comparison and a purity-adjusted regression (immune ~ chemo + purity), and state whether the conclusion changes.
briefing.reason: A purity difference between groups could pass for an immune difference.

briefing.text: Immune scores can depend on processing batch. Cross-tabulate PROCESSING_BATCH by chemo status and compare IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE across batches. If batch is unbalanced, include it as a covariate or stratum, or compare within batch. Do not batch-correct in a way that removes the chemo signal when batch and chemo are confounded.
briefing.reason: A batch artefact can create or hide a group difference.

briefing.text: Hospital SITE may differ in both chemotherapy practice and assay handling. Cross-tabulate SITE by chemo status and compare immune scores by site, and adjust for or stratify by site if it is associated. Lab variables unrelated to the hypothesis (e.g. glucose, haemoglobin, creatinine) are distractors: do not add them to models without a reason.
briefing.reason: Site is a possible confounder or source of clustering. Unrelated covariates only add noise.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat PRIOR_CHEMOTHERAPY (as decoded, verified against PRIOR_CHEMO_CYCLES) as a binary exposure and assume a single mean shift is the right summary; neither tested whether the difference scales with the number of cycles, which would distinguish a real exposure effect from a coding or grouping artefact.

Both assume the expression sample reflects the patient's state after any prior chemotherapy (i.e., the sample was taken after treatment). The sample table has no collection date, so whether 'prior' refers to before sampling or before enrolment was not examined.
Both assume the batch effect is purely additive and that adjusting for it is enough; neither checked whether the large batch shifts interact with chemo group or sample type.
Both assume that one sample per patient and a 1:1:1 merge mean records are independent; site-level clustering was adjusted for by team A only.
unused_evidence: PRIOR_CHEMO_CYCLES was used only to check the coding, not as a dose-response check of the immune difference.
STROMAL_SCORE, a second expression-derived signature that, like the immune score, depends on purity and batch, was not used as a negative/positive control or covariate.

ECOG_PS, FOLLOW_UP_MONTHS, AGE, SEX and patient labs (glucose, haemoglobin, creatinine) were not checked for imbalance between chemo groups; pretreated patients may differ systematically (e.g., more advanced disease).
Team B did not use SITE at all (team A did).
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named reliance on the description line as their weakest point; both resolved it with an exact cross-tab against cycles (0 disagreements), so this is resolved rather than only reported.
Team A reported a Hessian warning in the mixed model and set it aside as redundant; this is reasonable with one sample per patient but was not shown.
Team B listed no pitfalls in pitfalls_checked and did not report a purity-by-chemo comparison or site adjustment in its notes, though its OLS includes purity.
second_readings: 'Higher immune infiltration score' could be read as the raw score or as the purity-adjusted score (immune infiltration relative to non-tumour content); both teams report raw and purity-adjusted results, which agree in direction.
'Received prior chemotherapy' could mean any cycles versus a substantial course; a cycles-based dose-response reading could be checked.

Group of interest: all samples versus primary tumours only (metastases may be sampled after chemotherapy for different reasons); team A reports a primary-only analysis, team B reports only sample-type adjustment.
challenge.verdict: Fairly high trust. Both teams decoded the inverted chemo flag and confirmed it exactly against cycles, and the difference is large, holds after adjustment and points the same way in every stratum. Remaining gaps are untested dose-response, unused clinical covariates and the stromal signature, and team B's missing site adjustment; none of these looks likely to reverse the result, but they have not been checked.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Among patients who received prior chemotherapy, does IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE vary with PRIOR_CHEMO_CYCLES (e.g., by cycle-count bins or a regression on cycles, adjusted as in your main model)? Does the pattern support treating chemo as a binary exposure, and does it change your method or confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Run the same chemo comparison on STROMAL_SCORE and check whether ECOG_PS, AGE, FOLLOW_UP_MONTHS and SITE are balanced between chemo groups. If the stromal score or any of these differ by chemo group, does adding them to the model or stratifying on them change the direction or size of the immune difference?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Fit an interaction of chemo group with PROCESSING_BATCH and with SAMPLE_TYPE. Is the chemo difference homogeneous across them, or is it concentrated in particular cells? Does this change how you summarise the result?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your notes do not include SITE or a direct comparison of TUMOR_PURITY between chemo groups. Cross-tabulate chemo by SITE, compare purity between groups, and refit your adjusted model with SITE added. Does the estimate or its direction change?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Among patients who received prior chemotherapy, does IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE vary with PRIOR_CHEMO_CYCLES? Does the shape of that relation support your binary comparison, and does it change your method or confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Repeat the comparison separately in primary-tumour and metastasis samples, and on STROMAL_SCORE as a parallel signature. Also check ECOG_PS and AGE balance across chemo groups. Do any of these results change your method or the strength of your conclusion?

questions.why: Neither team used the cycles variable beyond checking the coding; a standard dose-response check would strengthen or weaken the binary conclusion.

findings.question: In bulk-expression immune signature scores (e.g., ESTIMATE-type immune scores), is there a documented, typical direction of change in immune infiltration in tumour samples taken after neoadjuvant or prior systemic chemotherapy compared with treatment-naive samples?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (3 used), so no pages were read. From prior knowledge only: no single typical direction exists. Many paired pre/post neoadjuvant studies report more TILs or immune signatures after chemotherapy (immunogenic cell death). Others report immune depletion or a shift towards suppressive cells. Post-treatment fibrosis or stroma also lowers tumour purity, which inflates ESTIMATE immune scores. Either direction is plausible, so a strong effect should prompt checks for purity, sample-type and batch artefacts.

findings.question: When a binary treatment flag and a treatment-count variable are both available, what is the recommended practice for checking for a dose-response as support for an exposure effect in observational cohort analyses?
findings.answer: The web did not settle this (gateway HTTP 403; no pages read). Standard epidemiological practice (Bradford Hill's biological gradient criterion) is as follows. First check that count==0 matches the unexposed flag. Then test for a trend of the outcome across ordered exposure levels (0, low, high cycles, or cycles as a continuous variable) using a regression trend test or Spearman/Jonckheere-Terpstra, adjusting for the same covariates as the main analysis, and optionally restricting to exposed patients. A monotone gradient supports an exposure effect. Its absence weakens the effect but does not refute it, because of threshold effects and confounding by indication.
